These components are standardized for G5 miniature bi-pin bases and are often sold in multi-packs for better value if you are repairing multiple fixtures.

  • Safety: Always turn off the power at the breaker before replacing these components.

For the best overall value and reliability, the Leviton T5 Turn-Type Lampholder is recommended due to its high user ratings and robust safety certifications.

In the context of lighting, shunted refers to how electrical current flows through the metal contacts (pins) of a lamp holder (tombstone).

Shunted vs. Non-Shunted

The primary difference lies in whether the two contacts for a single bulb end are internally connected or kept separate.

  • Shunted Lamp Holders: These have internal wiring that connects the two contacts together. This creates a single path for the electrical current to flow through. They are most commonly used with Instant Start ballasts.
  • Non-Shunted Lamp Holders: These keep the two contacts isolated from each other, providing two separate paths for the current. These are required for Programmed Start or Rapid Start ballasts, which need to send a specific voltage through the lamp's filaments to warm them up before lighting.

How to Tell the Difference

You usually cannot tell just by looking at the outside of the socket. The most reliable way to check is using a multimeter to test for continuity between the two pin holes. If the meter beeps, it is shunted; if there is no continuity, it is non-shunted.

Why It Matters for Your T5 Fixture

When you are buying replacement end caps like the ones you were looking at, getting the wrong type can cause issues:

  • Using Shunted in a Non-Shunted Fixture: This will likely cause a short circuit, which can instantly burn out a new ballast.
  • Using Non-Shunted in a Shunted Fixture: The light simply won't turn on because the electrical circuit remains open.

Since you are looking at T5 fixtures, these almost exclusively use non-shunted sockets because T5 ballasts are typically "Programmed Start" to preserve bulb life.

turns.prompt_text: because the ballast I'm using are ultraviolet light I believe they should not be shunted
turns.response_html:
You are correct. Ultraviolet (UV) ballasts typically use Programmed Start or Preheat technology, which requires non-shunted end caps.

Since UV bulbs have delicate filaments, they need two separate electrical paths—one for each pin—to warm up before the high-voltage arc strikes. Using a shunted holder would bridge these paths, causing the ballast to short-circuit or the bulb to fail prematurely.

Verification for UV Use

When installing these for UV lamps, keep these two things in mind:

  1. Wire Entry Points: Look at the back of the socket. A non-shunted socket will have two separate entry points for wires (one for each pin). A shunted socket often has only one or the two are internally bridged.
  2. Material: UV light can degrade some plastics over time. The flame-retardant and heat-resistant materials in the Harfington 24-Pack are better suited for the high-intensity environment of UV lighting.

For the best overall value and a secure, vibration-resistant fit for your UV bulbs, I recommend the Harfington T5 Non-Shunted Light Holder (24 Pack).

Most T5 non-shunted sockets are designed for 18 AWG solid wire, which is the standard for ballast bypass and lighting repairs. If you use stranded wire, just be sure to tin the tips with your soldering iron first to ensure they slide into the push-in terminals securely and don't fray.

If you decide to go with the Harfington 24-Pack, they are particularly forgiving with wire thickness due to their robust internal copper contacts.
